story: In 1991, Benin became the first country in mainland Africa where a sitting ruler lost an election and handed over power peacefully. For a generation it was held up as proof that the continent's "Big Man" era could end. In 2026 it held another orderly transfer of power, and almost nobody outside the government treated it as a celebration.

President Patrice Talon stepped down after two terms, as the constitution requires. His handpicked successor, finance minister Romuald Wadagni, won the 12 April election with 94.05 percent. His only opponent took under 6 percent because the main opposition party, Les Démocrates, was kept off the ballot (KAS). In January's parliamentary vote the same party fell short of a 20 percent threshold, leaving Talon's coalition with every seat (Al Jazeera). The vote came four months after a coup attempt in December 2025 that was put down with help from Nigerian troops, and with jihadists of JNIM pressing into the north, where they killed 54 soldiers at one post in 2025. Talon's defenders point to roads, ports and fiscal discipline; his critics point to rules rewritten since 2016 so that his camp could not lose. Benin shows that democracy can erode without a coup: through thresholds, candidate rules and an election whose result everyone knew in advance.
briefing.power: A presidential republic. The president is directly elected for five years with a two-term limit and heads the government; the National Assembly is elected by proportional representation with high party thresholds.
briefing.holders: President Romuald Wadagni, Talon's successor, in office since May 2026.
